linux-cli-001.question: Which of the following correctly pairs standard Linux directories with what is placed in them?
choices: /etc: configuration files of the system and services; /var/log: log files; /usr/bin: executables of the commands users run
/etc: executables of the commands users run; /var/log: log files; /usr/bin: configuration files of the system and services
/etc: configuration files of the system and services; /var/log: log files; /usr/bin: each user's personal files
linux-cli-001.explanation: The directory layout of Linux broadly follows a convention called the FHS (Filesystem Hierarchy Standard). /etc holds configuration files of the system and services, /var/log holds log files, and /usr/bin holds the executables of commands users run, such as ls and grep. Each user's personal files live in that user's home directory under /home. Temporary files that may be lost at a reboot go in /tmp.
choiceNotes: Correct. Configuration is in /etc, logs in /var/log and commands in /usr/bin.
The roles of /etc and /usr/bin are swapped. Command executables are in /usr/bin and configuration files in /etc.
Each user's personal files are kept in the home directories under /home.

linux-cli-002.question: Which of the following correctly describes the /proc directory on Linux?
choices: It is a write-protected place (for ordinary users) that collects the configuration files the kernel and services read at boot
It is where device files are placed, which represent devices such as hard disks, USB drives and terminals so that they can be read and written like files
It is a virtual file system through which the kernel shows running processes and the system state as files; its contents are not stored on disk
linux-cli-002.explanation: /proc is a virtual file system called procfs: each time a file is read, the kernel generates the information as of that moment. cat /proc/cpuinfo shows the CPU model and number of cores, cat /proc/meminfo shows memory usage, and /proc/<process ID>/ holds information on each process. Because the files do not exist on disk, many of them are shown with a size of 0. It is also often used on servers that run EDA tools, to check the number of CPU cores and the amount of memory.
choiceNotes: Configuration files are kept in /etc. /proc is not a place for storing files.
Device files are kept in /dev (/dev/sda, /dev/null and so on).
Correct. It is a virtual file system whose contents the kernel generates each time they are read.

linux-cli-003.question: The directory /home/alice/data exists, and the current directory is /home/alice/work. Which of the following is the directory shown when "cd ../data" is run and then "pwd"?
choices: /data
/home/alice/data
/home/alice/work/data
linux-cli-003.explanation: A path that does not start with "/" is a relative path and is interpreted starting from the current directory. ".." means the parent directory, so .. moves from /home/alice/work to /home/alice, and data then leads into /home/alice/data. pwd prints the current directory as an absolute path starting with "/". An absolute path starting with "/" always refers to the same place regardless of the current directory.
choiceNotes: /data is the data directory directly under the root directory. A relative path is interpreted from the current directory, not from "/".
Correct. .. moves to /home/alice, and from there into data.
/home/alice/work/data is where "cd data" would go. ".." means going back to the parent directory.

linux-cli-004.question: In the home directory, "ls" shows only notes.txt, while "ls -a" shows ".", "..", ".bashrc" and "notes.txt". Which of the following correctly explains this result?
choices: "." means the current directory and ".." the parent directory; .bashrc, whose name starts with ".", is a hidden file and is not shown without -a
"." means the current directory and ".." the parent directory; .bashrc is a write-protected file and is not shown without -a
"." means the root directory and ".." the home directory; .bashrc, whose name starts with ".", is a hidden file and is not shown without -a
linux-cli-004.explanation: Every directory contains an entry "." for the directory itself and ".." for its parent. Files and directories whose names start with "." are treated as hidden: ls does not show them without options, and shows them with -a (all). Configuration files of shells and tools, such as .bashrc, are often given hidden names so that they do not clutter ordinary listings. Whether a file is shown depends only on its name and has nothing to do with its permissions.
choiceNotes: Correct. Both the meaning of "." and ".." and the handling of hidden files are described correctly.
Whether ls shows a file depends on whether its name starts with ".", not on write permission.
The root directory is written "/" and the home directory "~". "." and ".." are the directory itself and its parent.

linux-cli-005.question: When the commands above are run in order, which of the following is the result of the last two cat commands?
linux-cli-005.code:
$ echo hello > a.txt
$ ln a.txt h.txt
$ ln -s a.txt s.txt
$ rm a.txt
$ cat h.txt
$ cat s.txt
choices: Both h.txt and s.txt show hello
h.txt gives an error that the file is not found, and s.txt shows hello
h.txt shows hello, and s.txt gives an error that the file is not found
linux-cli-005.explanation: A hard link made with ln is another name that points to the same inode (the numbered record that manages a file's contents and attributes) as the original file. rm a.txt removes only the name a.txt; because the name h.txt remains, the contents are not deleted and cat h.txt shows hello. A symbolic link made with ln -s is a separate file whose contents are the path "a.txt", so once a.txt is gone there is nothing to follow and cat s.txt gives a "No such file or directory" error. A symbolic link whose target has disappeared stays behind as a broken (dangling) link.
choiceNotes: A symbolic link opens the file by following its path, so once a.txt is gone it cannot be read through s.txt.
The behavior of hard links and symbolic links is reversed. As long as one name remains, the contents can be read through a hard link.
Correct. A hard link is a name for the same inode and survives, while the symbolic link becomes broken.

linux-cli-006.question: A directory contains six files: a1.txt, a2.txt, a10.txt, b1.txt, c1.txt and a1.csv. Which of the following is the number of files shown when "ls [ab]?.txt" is run in this directory?
linux-cli-006.explanation: Before running a command, the shell expands names containing wildcards into file names (globbing). [ab] matches one character that is either a or b, ? matches exactly one character, and * matches any string of zero or more characters. [ab]?.txt means "a or b, then any one character, then .txt", so it matches the three files a1.txt, a2.txt and b1.txt. a10.txt has two characters after a, c1.txt starts with c, and a1.csv has a different extension, so they do not match.
choiceNotes: [ab] matches one character that is a or b, so b1.txt is included too.
Correct. The three files are a1.txt, a2.txt and b1.txt.
? matches exactly one character, so a10.txt is not included. Reading ? as zero or more characters, like *, would include a10.txt and give 4.

linux-cli-007.question: After "chmod 754 run.sh" is run on the file run.sh, which of the following is the permission notation shown at the start of the line from "ls -l run.sh"?
choices: -rwxr-xr--
-r--r-xrwx
-rwxrw-r--
linux-cli-007.explanation: Octal permissions are ordered, from the left, owner (user), group and others, and each digit is the sum of read r = 4, write w = 2 and execute x = 1. 7 = 4 + 2 + 1 is rwx, 5 = 4 + 1 is r-x and 4 is r--, so 754 becomes rwxr-xr--. The leading "-" means a regular file; a directory would show "d". With this setting the owner can read, write and execute, the group can read and execute, and other users can only read.
choiceNotes: Correct. 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x and 4 is r--.
This reads the three digits in reverse order and corresponds to chmod 457. The octal digits are owner, group and others from the left.
5 is 4 + 1, that is r-x. rw- corresponds to 4 + 2 = 6.

linux-cli-008.question: touch creates a new file from 666, and mkdir a new directory from 777, with the umask bits removed. Which of the following is the correct pair of permissions when a new file and a new directory are created in a shell whose umask is 027?
choices: file 637, directory 750
file 640, directory 750
file 750, directory 750
linux-cli-008.explanation: The umask gives the permission bits to "remove" from newly created files and directories. 027 removes write (2) from the group and read, write and execute (7) from others, so a file becomes rw-r----- (640) from 666 and a directory becomes rwxr-x--- (750) from 777. This is not octal subtraction but bitwise removal (666 AND NOT 027). With the commonly used umask 022, the same calculation gives 644 for files and 755 for directories.
choiceNotes: This is 027 subtracted from 666 in octal. The umask removes bits one by one, so the result can differ from subtraction (with 022 both give 644).
Correct. A file goes from 666 to 640 and a directory from 777 to 750.
Files are created from 666, not 777, so a new file does not get execute permission.

linux-cli-009.question: The directory d has permissions rwx--x--x (711), and the file f.txt in it has rw-r--r-- (644). A user who is neither the owner nor the superuser runs "ls d" and "cat d/f.txt". Which of the following is the result?
choices: ls d shows the listing, but cat d/f.txt is not permitted because the directory permissions are insufficient
Neither ls d nor cat d/f.txt is permitted
ls d is not permitted, but cat d/f.txt shows the contents
linux-cli-009.explanation: For a directory, r is permission to read the list of names in it, and x is permission to enter it and reach a file by name. Others have only x, so ls d gives "Permission denied", but d/f.txt, whose name is known, can be reached. f.txt itself grants r to others, so cat can show its contents. Conversely, in a directory with r but no x, the names can be listed but the files in it cannot be opened.
choiceNotes: This is the result for a directory with r but without x. For 711, others have only x, so the listing cannot be read.
With x on the directory, a file can be reached by name. Whether it can be opened is decided by the permissions of f.txt itself.
Correct. In a directory with only x, files whose names are known can be opened even though the listing cannot be seen.

linux-cli-010.question: Which of the following correctly describes the sudo command on Linux?
choices: Anyone who knows the root password can run a command prefixed with sudo, and no record of who ran it is kept anywhere
A command prefixed with sudo is given a higher priority by the kernel than other processes and runs faster because it can use the CPU first
It lets a user permitted in sudoers run a command with the privileges of another user (root by default), and by default the user enters their own password
linux-cli-010.explanation: root is the administrator account (superuser) that can operate everything on the system, essentially without the restrictions of file permissions. sudo is a mechanism that lets only users permitted in /etc/sudoers or similar run individual commands with the privileges of root or another user; by default it confirms with the user's own password and records the commands run. Compared with sharing the root password and always logging in as root, it makes it easier to trace who did what, and strong privileges are used only when needed. Keeping privileges to the minimum necessary is based on the principle of least privilege in security.
choiceNotes: Only users permitted in sudoers can use sudo, and with the default settings the commands run are recorded.
Changing processing priority is done with nice or renice. sudo changes privileges and does not change speed.
Correct. A permitted user runs only the needed commands with another user's privileges.

linux-cli-011.question: On many Linux systems, "ls -l /usr/bin/passwd" shows "-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ...". Which of the following is the meaning of the "s" in the owner's execute position?
choices: setuid is set, so whoever runs it, the program runs with the privileges of the file's owner (here root)
The sticky bit is set, so users other than the owner and root cannot delete or rename this file
It indicates that this file is a shared library, which is only called from other programs and cannot be run directly as a command
linux-cli-011.explanation: s means that both the setuid (set user ID) bit and execute permission are set, and the program runs with the privileges of the file's owner rather than of the user who ran it. passwd must update /etc/shadow, which only root can write, when an ordinary user changes their own password, so it is a setuid-root program. A flaw in a setuid program can become a foothold for an ordinary user to gain root privileges, so the bit must not be set carelessly. In octal it is the 4000 place, and chmod 4755 gives -rwsr-xr-x.
choiceNotes: Correct. It runs with the privileges of the owner, root, rather than of the user who ran it.
The sticky bit is shown as "t" in the others' execute position (drwxrwxrwt for /tmp, for example). Set on a directory, it lets only the owner and a few others delete files in it.
Whether a file is a shared library does not appear in the permission notation. s is a mark about the privileges used when the file is run.

linux-cli-012.question: When the commands above are run in order, which of the following is the content shown by the last cat?
linux-cli-012.code:
$ echo a > f.txt
$ echo b > f.txt
$ echo c >> f.txt
$ cat f.txt
choices: Only the one line c
The two lines b and c
The three lines a, b and c
linux-cli-012.explanation: ">" is a redirection that writes output to a file; if the file already exists, it is emptied before writing (overwritten). ">>" appends to the end of the file. The first line writes a, the ">" in the second line leaves only b, and the ">>" in the third line adds c after it, so f.txt contains the two lines b and c. To avoid wiping out an important file with >, bash can forbid overwriting with set -o noclobber.
choiceNotes: ">>" appends rather than overwrites, so the b written in the second line remains.
Correct. > leaves only b, and >> appends c.
The ">" in the second line empties the file before writing, so the a from the first line does not remain.

linux-cli-013.question: As shown above, in a directory where a.txt exists and nofile does not, the last command is run. Which of the following is the result?
linux-cli-013.code:
$ ls
a.txt
$ ls a.txt nofile 2>&1 > out.txt
choices: Only the error line is written to out.txt, and the a.txt line is shown on the screen
Both the error line and the a.txt line are written to out.txt, and nothing is shown on the screen
Only the a.txt line is written to out.txt, and the error line is shown on the screen
linux-cli-013.explanation: Redirections are processed from left to right. "2>&1" means "send standard error (2) to where standard output (1) goes at that moment", and at that point standard output is still the screen, so errors appear on the screen. The following "> out.txt" changes only standard output to out.txt, so the file receives only the a.txt line, which is the normal output of ls. To write both to the file, change standard output first and then write 2>&1, as in "ls a.txt nofile > out.txt 2>&1".
choiceNotes: 2>&1 points standard error to where standard output goes "at that moment", that is, the screen. The error does not go into out.txt.
This is the result when written in the order "> out.txt 2>&1". Swapping the order changes the result.
Correct. At the time of 2>&1 standard output is the screen, so the error appears on the screen.

linux-cli-014.question: In the session above, which of the following is the value printed by the last command?
linux-cli-014.code:
$ cat log.txt
INFO start
ERROR disk full
warning: error retry
Error: error twice
INFO done
$ grep -ic error log.txt
linux-cli-014.explanation: grep's -i means ignoring the difference between upper and lower case, and -c means printing the "number of lines" that match. The lines containing error regardless of case are the three lines ERROR disk full, warning: error retry and Error: error twice, so the output is 3. error appears twice in the fourth line, but -c counts lines, so it is counted as 1. Other frequently used options are -v to print non-matching lines, -r to search through subdirectories as well and -n to add line numbers.
choiceNotes: This is the value without -i. With -i, the lines containing ERROR and Error are counted too.
Correct. Three lines contain error when case is ignored.
This counts the matches (error appears 4 times). -c counts the number of matching lines.

linux-cli-015.question: In the session above, which of the following are the lines printed by the last grep?
linux-cli-015.code:
$ cat words.txt
bat
bt
boat
abet
bit.txt
$ grep '^b.t' words.txt
choices: bat, bit.txt
bat, abet, bit.txt
bat, bt, boat, bit.txt
linux-cli-015.explanation: In a regular expression, ^ means the start of a line, . any single character and $ the end of a line. ^b.t means "b at the start of the line, then any one character, then t", so it matches bat and bit.txt. bt has no character between b and t, and in boat the character two after b is a, so they do not match. In abet the part bet fits b.t, but the line starts with a, so it fails the ^ condition.
choiceNotes: Correct. bat and bit.txt are the lines with b, any one character and t from the start of the line.
This is the result without ^ (grep 'b.t'). With ^, only lines that start with b match.
This is the result of reading . like .* (any string of zero or more characters). . matches exactly one character.

linux-cli-016.question: The choices omit the leading spaces of the line. In the session above, which of the following is the line printed by the last pipeline?
linux-cli-016.explanation: sort arranges the lines so that identical lines are adjacent, and uniq -c merges adjacent identical lines and adds counts, giving the three lines 3 10.0.0.5, 2 10.0.0.9 and 1 10.0.0.2. sort -nr sorts by the leading number in descending order and head -n 1 takes the first line, so the output is 3 10.0.0.5. uniq merges only "adjacent" identical lines, so sorting first is essential. Chaining commands with pipes like this is a standard way to count the IP addresses with the most accesses, or the most frequent errors, in a log.
choiceNotes: Without -r on the last sort, the lines are in ascending order and the first is 1 10.0.0.2. -r sorts in descending order.
This is the result of counting with uniq -c alone, without the first sort. uniq merges only adjacent lines, so only the two consecutive 10.0.0.9 lines are counted as 2.
Correct. 10.0.0.5 appears most often, 3 times.

linux-cli-017.question: You want to keep showing lines on the screen as they are appended later to the server log file /var/log/app.log. Which of the following commands is appropriate?
choices: tail -f /var/log/app.log
head -n 10 /var/log/app.log
cat /var/log/app.log
linux-cli-017.explanation: tail shows the last lines of a file (10 by default); with -f (follow) it does not exit after showing them but keeps watching the file and shows appended lines as they arrive. It is often used to follow the progress of a simulation or job through its log, and Ctrl+C stops it. When the log is rotated to a different name, tail -F, which keeps following a new file with the same name, is convenient. head shows the first lines and cat the whole file once, and then they exit.
choiceNotes: Correct. With -f it keeps showing appended lines.
head -n 10 shows the first 10 lines once and does not show appended lines.
cat shows the contents at that moment once and exits; it does not show lines appended later.

linux-cli-018.question: Which of the following is the output of the command above, which extracts columns from a comma-separated line?
choices: ALU 0.82
ALU,TT,0.82
linux-cli-018.explanation: cut's -d specifies the delimiter and -f the numbers of the fields to extract. With -d, making the comma the delimiter, 2026-10-01 is field 1, ALU field 2, TT field 3 and 0.82 field 4. -f2,4 means fields 2 and 4, so the output is ALU,0.82. The original delimiter is kept between the extracted fields.
choiceNotes: cut puts the original delimiter (a comma here) between the extracted fields. It does not replace it with a space.
Correct. Fields 2 and 4 are printed, joined by a comma.
This is the output of "-f2-4", which extracts fields 2 through 4. "2,4" means only fields 2 and 4.

linux-cli-019.question: Which of the following is the output of the sed command above, which replaces characters?
choices: xaa bab
xaa bxb
xxx bxb
linux-cli-019.explanation: sed's s/before/after/ replaces only the first match found on each line. The first a on this line is the first character, so the output is xaa bab. To replace every match on the line, add g (global) at the end, as in s/a/x/g, which outputs xxx bxb. Replacement works line by line, so if a file has several lines, the first match on each line is replaced even without g.
choiceNotes: Correct. Without g, only the first a on the line becomes x.
Replacement is done per line, not per word. Without g, only the first match on the line is replaced.
This is the output with g added, as in s/a/x/g.

linux-cli-020.question: In the session above, which of the following is printed by the last awk?
linux-cli-020.code:
$ cat result.txt
cellA PASS 0.12
cellB FAIL 0.45
cellC PASS 0.08
cellD FAIL 0.31
$ awk '$2 == "FAIL" {print $1}' result.txt
choices: The two lines cellB FAIL 0.45 and cellD FAIL 0.31
The two lines FAIL and FAIL
The two lines cellB and cellD
linux-cli-020.explanation: awk splits each line at blanks into fields, written $1 for the first, $2 for the second and so on, with $0 for the whole line. "$2 == "FAIL"" is a pattern that selects lines whose second field is FAIL, and {print $1} is the action that prints the first field of such a line. The matching lines are those of cellB and cellD, so cellB and cellD are printed. awk treats a run of blanks as a single separator, so it can be easier than cut for extracting columns from output with uneven spacing.
choiceNotes: This is the result without {print $1}. If the action is omitted, the whole matching line ($0) is printed.
This reads the fields as counted from 0. In awk, $1 is the first field and $0 is the whole line.
Correct. The first field of each line whose second field is FAIL is printed.

linux-cli-021.question: Which of the following describes the files found when find /data -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -size +100M is run with GNU find?
choices: Files whose names end in .log, last modified 8 or more days ago, and larger than 100 MiB
Files whose names end in .log, last modified within 7 days, and larger than 100 MiB
Files whose names end in .log, created 8 or more days ago, and larger than 100 MiB
linux-cli-021.explanation: -name "*.log" selects names ending in .log, -mtime the time the contents were last modified, and -size +100M sizes larger than 100 MiB. -mtime compares the elapsed time counted in 24-hour units with the fraction discarded, so +7 means "more than 7", that is, 8 days (192 hours) or more; a file only 7 days and 23 hours old is not selected. Files modified within 7 days are selected with -mtime -7. *.log is quoted so that the shell does not expand it first into file names in the current directory.
choiceNotes: Correct. +7 means a day count, with the fraction discarded, greater than 7, that is, 8 or more days.
Selecting files modified within 7 days is -mtime -7. + means "more than" and - means "less than".
-mtime compares the time the contents were last modified, not the time the file was created.

linux-cli-022.question: When stopping a process that has stopped responding, it is recommended to first use "kill <process ID>" and to use "kill -9 <process ID>" only if that does not end it. Which of the following is the reason?
choices: The default SIGTERM (number 15) can be received by the process so that it can clean up before exiting, whereas SIGKILL (number 9) cannot be received and ends it forcibly without cleanup
SIGTERM (number 15), which kill sends by default, ends everything including child processes, whereas SIGKILL (number 9) ends only the specified process and so has less impact
SIGKILL (number 9) can be received by the process so that it can clean up before exiting, whereas SIGTERM (number 15), which kill sends by default, cannot be ignored and ends it at once
linux-cli-022.explanation: A signal is a short notification by which the OS tells a process about an event, and each has a fixed number and name. Without options, kill sends SIGTERM (number 15); a program can provide a routine (handler) that receives it, saving files in progress or deleting temporary files before exiting. SIGKILL (number 9) can be neither received nor ignored by the process, and the kernel ends it forcibly, so half-written files may be left corrupted. The ID of the process to stop is found with ps or top.
choiceNotes: Correct. SIGTERM gives a chance to clean up, while SIGKILL ends the process forcibly.
Both signals are sent to the specified process. Whether child processes also end is not decided by the type of signal.
The behavior of SIGTERM and SIGKILL is reversed. The one that can be received for cleanup is SIGTERM.

linux-cli-023.question: While a long-running ./sim.sh is running in a terminal, you want to use other commands in the same terminal. Which of the following is what happens when you press Ctrl+Z and then run bg?
choices: Ctrl+Z ends sim.sh, and running bg starts the same command again from the beginning in the background
Ctrl+Z suspends sim.sh, and bg resumes it from where it stopped, in the background
Ctrl+Z moves sim.sh to the background where it keeps running, and running bg suspends it
linux-cli-023.explanation: Pressing Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP to the job running in the foreground, and the job is suspended. bg tells that job to resume and continue in the background, and fg brings it back to the foreground. The jobs and their states can be checked with jobs, and to run something in the background from the start, it is launched with &, as in "./sim.sh &". However, background jobs may also stop when the terminal connection is lost, so long-running work needs a separate measure.
choiceNotes: Ctrl+Z suspends the job rather than ending it. bg resumes it from where it stopped, not from the beginning.
Correct. bg resumes the suspended job in the background.
The roles of Ctrl+Z and bg are reversed. Ctrl+Z suspends, and bg resumes in the background.

linux-cli-024.question: On a server reached over SSH, a long-running task was started with "./run.sh &", and when the connection was closed the task stopped too. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to start it so that it keeps running after the connection is closed?
choices: ./run.sh > run.log 2>&1 &
nice -n 19 ./run.sh > run.log 2>&1 &
nohup ./run.sh > run.log 2>&1 &
linux-cli-024.explanation: When the connection is lost, SIGHUP, which reports that the terminal has hung up, is sent to the shell, and shells such as bash also send SIGHUP to their jobs. The default action on receiving SIGHUP is to exit, so background jobs stop as well. nohup starts the command so that it ignores SIGHUP, and with its output directed to a file, the task keeps running after the connection is closed. If it is started from a terminal without redirecting the output, nohup writes the output to a file called nohup.out. Another common approach is to use a tool such as tmux or screen, which keeps the terminal session alive on the server and lets you reattach to it later.
choiceNotes: Directing the output to a file does not stop the task from exiting when it receives SIGHUP.
nice -n 19 only starts the task with a lower priority and does not change how it reacts to SIGHUP.
Correct. nohup makes it ignore SIGHUP, and the output is kept in a file.

linux-cli-025.question: When the two lines above are run in a shell, which of the following are the characters shown?
linux-cli-025.code:
$ false && echo A || echo B
$ true || echo C; echo D
choices: Only D
B and D
B, C and D
linux-cli-025.explanation: Every command returns an exit status when it finishes: 0 means success and anything other than 0 means failure (the last value can be seen with $?). "A && B" runs B only if A succeeds, "A || B" runs B only if A fails, and ";" runs the next command regardless of the result. In the first line false fails, so echo A is skipped, the whole "false && echo A" is treated as a failure, and echo B after || is run. In the second line true succeeds, so echo C is not run, while echo D after ";" always runs, so B and D are shown.
choiceNotes: echo B in the first line is also run. After && skips its command, the result is still a failure, so the part after || runs.
Correct. B is shown by the first line and D by the second.
|| runs the right-hand command only when the left one fails. true succeeds, so echo C is not run.

linux-cli-026.question: When the commands above are run in order, which of the following is the output of the two echo commands?
choices: The first is Hello world and the second Hello $name
Both the first and the second are Hello world
The first is Hello $name and the second Hello world
linux-cli-026.explanation: In the shell, a part enclosed in single quotes ('...') is taken literally, and variables such as $name are not expanded. Inside double quotes ("...") variables are expanded, so the second becomes Hello world. Double quotes are also used to make a variable's value a single argument even if it contains spaces. Note that in the assignment "name=world", no spaces may be placed around the =.
choiceNotes: The roles of single and double quotes are reversed. Variables are expanded inside double quotes.
Variables are not expanded inside single quotes.
Correct. Single quotes keep the text as is, and double quotes expand variables.

linux-cli-027.question: As shown above, the script s.sh is run with arguments. Which of the following is the output?
linux-cli-027.code:
$ cat s.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "$# $1"
$ ./s.sh a "b c" d
choices: 3 ./s.sh
3 a
4 a
linux-cli-027.explanation: Inside a script, $1, $2, ... are the first, second, ... arguments, $# is the number of arguments and $0 is the name of the script itself. "b c" is enclosed in double quotes, so it becomes one argument containing a space, and there are three arguments: a, b c and d. Therefore $# is 3 and $1 is a, and the output is 3 a. To pass all the arguments to another command while keeping them separate, "$@" is written.
choiceNotes: The name of the script is $0; $1 is the first argument, a.
Correct. The three arguments are a, b c and d, and the first is a.
The quoted "b c" is a single argument, so there are 3 arguments, not 4.

linux-cli-028.question: In a shell script, in which of the following cases is the condition of the if above true?
choices: When a regular file with the name in variable f exists
When a file with the name in variable f exists and its size is greater than 0
When a file or a directory with the name in variable f exists
linux-cli-028.explanation: [ ] is another way of writing the test command: it returns exit status 0 (true) if the condition holds, and if branches on that. -f checks that "a regular file with that name exists" and is false for a directory. To check only existence, use -e; to check for a directory, -d; and to check that the size is greater than 0, -s. A space is required after [ and before ], and enclosing the variable in double quotes, as in "$f", makes the test work correctly even for names containing spaces.
choiceNotes: Correct. -f is true when a regular file exists, even if it is empty.
Checking that the size is greater than 0 as well is -s. -f is true even for an empty file.
Checking existence regardless of file or directory is -e. -f is false for a directory.

linux-cli-029.question: Which of the following are the files in the directory after the session above?
linux-cli-029.code:
$ ls
a.log  b.log  notes.txt
$ for f in *.log; do mv "$f" "${f%.log}.txt"; done
choices: a.log.txt, b.log.txt, notes.txt
Still a.log, b.log, notes.txt, with the string ".log" inside a.log and b.log replaced by ".txt"
a.txt, b.txt, notes.txt
linux-cli-029.explanation: for f in *.log puts a.log and b.log, which match *.log, into the variable f one at a time and repeats the part between do and done. ${f%.log} is the value of f with .log removed from the end, so for a.log it is a, and mv "$f" "${f%.log}.txt" renames a.log to a.txt. notes.txt does not match *.log and is left as is. "$f" is enclosed in double quotes so that a name containing spaces is passed to mv as a single argument.
choiceNotes: This is the result of writing mv "$f" "$f.txt". ${f%.log} removes the trailing .log.
mv renames files and does not change their contents. Replacing contents is done with sed and similar tools.
Correct. The names change to have the trailing .log removed and .txt added.

linux-cli-030.question: An executable script run.sh in the current directory gives "command not found" when run by typing "run.sh", but runs when typed as "./run.sh". Which of the following is the reason?
choices: run.sh has no execute permission, and only when ./ is put in front can it be run without permission
A command name without a slash is searched for only in the directories of the PATH environment variable, which generally does not include the current directory
The #!/bin/bash on the first line of run.sh (the shebang) is read only when it is run with ./ in front
linux-cli-030.explanation: When the shell receives a command name without a slash, it searches in order through the directories listed, separated by colons, in the PATH environment variable (/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin and so on) and runs what it finds. The current directory is generally not put in PATH, so that a malicious program with the same name placed elsewhere is not run by mistake. Writing a path containing a slash, such as ./run.sh, runs that file directly without searching PATH. The #!/bin/bash on the first line (the shebang) specifies the interpreter that runs the script, whichever way it is started.
choiceNotes: Without execute permission, ./run.sh also fails with "Permission denied".
Correct. The current directory is not in PATH, so its location must be given with ./.
Whether the script is found through PATH or started with ./, the kernel reads the shebang and runs the script with the specified interpreter.

linux-cli-031.question: When the commands above are run in order, which of the following is the pair of outputs of the two bash -c commands?
choices: [] and []
linux-cli-031.explanation: A variable that is only assigned, as in "X=1", is a shell variable: it can be used only inside that shell and is not passed to child processes it starts (here a new bash). With export it becomes an environment variable, and its value is inherited by child processes started afterwards. Therefore the first output is [] and the second [1]. Because of the single quotes, $X is expanded not in the parent shell but inside the child bash.
choiceNotes: Correct. Until it is exported, X is not passed to child processes.
A shell variable that is only assigned is not inherited by child processes.
Child processes started after export inherit the value of X.

linux-cli-032.question: Which of the following is the main function of a Linux package management system (apt on Debian-based systems, dnf on Red Hat-based systems and so on)?
choices: Bundling several files and directories into one compressed file so that they are easy to send to another computer
Always compiling the source code of the software on the spot and optimizing it for the CPU in use before installing it
Fetching software from repositories and managing installation, updates and removal, including the packages it depends on
linux-cli-032.explanation: A package management system handles software in units called packages, fetches them from distribution servers (repositories), and installs, updates and removes them. It automatically finds the other packages that a package needs in order to work (its dependencies) and installs them together, and it records the list of installed files so that removal and updates are clean. Installing into the system with apt or dnf generally requires root privileges, so they are run with sudo. Some software, such as commercial EDA tools, is installed with its own installer without going through the package management system.
choiceNotes: Bundling and compressing files is the job of tar, gzip, zip and the like.
Packages installed with apt or dnf are usually precompiled and are not compiled on the spot.
Correct. It manages installation, updates and removal, including dependencies.

linux-cli-033.question: On a Linux system using systemd, which of the following is the difference between "systemctl start license.service" and "systemctl enable license.service" for the service license.service?
choices: start makes the service run automatically from the next boot of the computer, and enable starts the service right now
start starts the service right now, and enable sets it to start automatically when the computer boots
start runs the service as one only root can use, and enable allows ordinary users to operate the service too
linux-cli-033.explanation: systemctl start starts the service right now, but the started state does not persist after a reboot. systemctl enable sets the service to be started automatically when the system boots, and enable alone does not start it now. To do both at once, use systemctl enable --now; stop stops it and disable removes the automatic start. Whether the service is running, and its recent log, can be checked with systemctl status.
choiceNotes: The roles of start and enable are reversed. start starts it immediately, and enable sets up automatic start at boot.
Correct. start starts it now, and enable sets up automatic start at boot.
start and enable do not decide who can operate the service.

linux-cli-034.question: The line "30 2 * * 1 /home/alice/backup.sh" was registered in cron. Which of the following is when backup.sh is run?
choices: At 2:30 on the 1st of every month
At 2:30 every Monday
At 2:30 every Sunday
linux-cli-034.explanation: In a cron configuration (crontab), each line starts with five fields that are, from the left, "minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week", followed by the command to run. In this line the minute is 30, the hour 2, the day of month and month * (every), and the day of week 1, so it runs at 2:30 every Monday. For the day of week, 0 is Sunday and 1 is Monday, and in many implementations 7 also means Sunday. Commands run from cron work with a limited set of environment variables, unlike a login session, so care is needed, such as writing commands in scripts with absolute paths.
choiceNotes: For the 1st of every month, set the third field, the day of month, to 1, as in "30 2 1 * *". The fifth field is the day of week.
Correct. It means minute 30, hour 2 and day of week 1 (Monday).
In the day-of-week field, 0 (or 7) is Sunday and 1 is Monday.

linux-cli-035.question: A Linux server warns that disk space is running low. Which of the following is the correct pair of a command to check usage and free space for each file system and a command to total the space used by the files in a directory?
choices: df and du
du and df
free and du
linux-cli-035.explanation: df (disk free) shows, for each mounted file system, its total size, used space and free space, and with -h it shows them readably in units such as G and M. du (disk usage) totals the space used by the files under a given directory, and used as in du -sh * it finds which directories are large. A standard procedure is to first find the full file system with df and then narrow down the large directories inside it with du. A file that has been deleted but is still held open by a process is counted as used by df but not by du, so the two values may not match.
choiceNotes: Correct. Free space per file system is checked with df, and the total used under a directory with du.
The roles of df and du are reversed.
free shows usage of memory (main memory and swap), not disk.

linux-cli-036.question: You created a public-key authentication key pair with ssh-keygen on your own PC and want to connect to the server server1 with ssh without a password. Which of the following is the correct way to place the keys?
choices: Add the private key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, and keep the public key only on your PC
Put both the public key and the private key in ~/.ssh on the server, and leave nothing on your PC
Add the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, and never let the private key leave your PC
linux-cli-036.explanation: In SSH public-key authentication, the server uses the public key registered in authorized_keys to confirm that the connecting side holds the corresponding private key. The private key itself is never sent, so it is kept only on your own PC, with permissions such as 600 so that others cannot read it, and protected by a passphrase. The public key (a .pub file such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub) may be known to others without harm, and ssh-copy-id adds it to the server's authorized_keys. The same key is also used when transferring files with scp or rsync, which run over ssh.
choiceNotes: As its name says, the private key must not leave your hands. What is registered on the server is the public key.
If the private key is placed on the server, anyone who can get into the server can use it. Also, without the private key at hand you cannot authenticate.
Correct. The public key is registered on the server, and the private key is protected at hand.

linux-cli-037.question: Which of the following is what happens when "tar -czf proj.tar.gz proj/" is run?
choices: It bundles the whole proj directory into one file and creates proj.tar.gz compressed with gzip
It extracts proj.tar.gz and puts the files it contains into the proj directory
It compresses each file in the proj directory one by one into separate .gz files
linux-cli-037.explanation: tar is a command that bundles several files and directories into one file (an archive): -c means create, -z compression with gzip, and -f that the following argument is the archive file name. The original proj directory remains as it is. To extract, use -x instead of -c, as in "tar -xzf proj.tar.gz", and to list the contents use -t. gzip alone only compresses a single file, so it is combined with tar to send a whole directory.
choiceNotes: Correct. -c creates the archive and -z applies gzip compression.
Extraction is done with -x. -c creates an archive.
Compressing files one by one into .gz is what gzip -r does. tar bundles them into one archive.

linux-cli-038.question: After editing main.c, a file managed with Git, only git commit -m "fix" was run, and "no changes added to commit" was shown and nothing was committed. Which of the following is the reason?
choices: Before committing, the changes have to be sent to the shared repository with git push
Changes to be included in a commit must first be registered in the staging area with git add
Git commits automatically when a file is saved, so there is no need to run git commit
linux-cli-038.explanation: In Git, of the changes edited in the working directory, only those registered in the staging area (the index) with git add are recorded by the next git commit. This two-step mechanism lets you pick only related changes out of several edits and make them one commit. git status shows which changes are staged. There is also git commit -a, which stages all changes to tracked files and commits them at once.
choiceNotes: git push sends commits to the shared repository and is used after committing.
Correct. Only changes staged with git add are committed.
Git does not commit automatically. The user decides which changes to record and when, with git add and git commit.

linux-cli-039.question: You ran git commit in Git, but the commit does not yet appear in the GitHub repository shared by the team. Which of the following is the reason?
choices: git commit only registers changes in the staging area, and git add is needed to record them
Sending committed changes to the shared repository requires running git pull
git commit records in the local repository, and git push is needed to send it to the remote
linux-cli-039.explanation: Git is a distributed version control system in which each developer has the whole repository locally, and git commit records changes in that local repository. To send them to a remote repository such as GitHub, git push is run; conversely, git pull (or git fetch and git merge) brings new remote commits into the local repository. This is why commits can be made without a network connection and pushed together later. If someone else has pushed first, you may be asked to bring in their changes first.
choiceNotes: The roles of git add and git commit are reversed. add stages and commit records.
git pull brings remote changes into the local repository; sending local commits is done with git push.
Correct. commit records locally, and push sends to the remote.

linux-cli-040.question: "build/" was written in the .gitignore of a project managed with Git, but changes to build/out.log, which was committed earlier, keep appearing in git status. Which of the following is the reason?
choices: .gitignore affects only files that are not yet tracked, so a tracked file must be removed from tracking with git rm --cached
Directories cannot be written in .gitignore, so the names of the files to ignore must be written one by one
.gitignore has no effect on any file until the .gitignore file itself is added with git add and committed
linux-cli-040.explanation: .gitignore is a setting that removes files that are not yet tracked (never committed or added with git add) from the git status listing and from what git add picks up. A file that is already tracked stays tracked even if it is written in .gitignore, so its changes keep appearing. git rm --cached build/out.log stops tracking it while keeping the file in the working directory, and after that is committed, the .gitignore entry takes effect. Large generated files such as simulation outputs and build results are best written in .gitignore from the start.
choiceNotes: Correct. .gitignore does not affect tracked files; git rm --cached removes them from tracking.
Writing it with a trailing slash, as in "build/", ignores the whole contents of a directory named build.
.gitignore takes effect as long as it is in the working directory, even if it is not committed. It is usually committed, however, so that the team shares the same settings.
